title: Solving problems with solids and plane shapes
canonical_examples_source: Arithmetic self-verified; method ref: NCERT Class 5/6 Maths; format ref: bank uk-ks2-2024 maths.

blocks.content: Once you know a shape's properties, you can use them to solve real problems — like how many faces to paint, or how a net folds into a solid.
Use a solid's properties to answer questions: a cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.

steps: To paint every face, you must paint all 6.

blocks.prompt: How many faces must you paint to cover a whole cube? ___
blocks.explain: A cube has 6 faces, so all 6 must be painted.
blocks.rule: Use the count of faces, edges or vertices to solve a problem about a solid.

blocks.content: A net is a flat pattern that folds up into a solid. A cube's net is made of 6 squares.

blocks.question: How many squares are in the net of a cube?
blocks.explain: A cube has 6 faces, so its net has 6 squares.
blocks.rule: A cube is made of 6 square faces, so its net has 6 squares.

blocks.question: A cuboid box has 6 faces. Ken says he only needs to measure 3 faces to know the sizes of all 6. Could he be right?
options: Yes — opposite faces of a cuboid are equal, so 3 different faces cover all 6
No, he must measure all 6 separately
blocks.explain: A cuboid's faces come in matching pairs: front and back, top and bottom, left and right. Each pair is equal, so measuring one of each pair (3 faces) tells him all 6. Spotting the pairs saves work.
blocks.rule: A cuboid's opposite faces are equal, forming 3 matching pairs.
blocks.principle: Symmetry in a solid means some measurements are repeated.
canonical_solution: They form 3 pairs of equal opposite faces

misconceptions.coach: Opposite faces are equal, so 3 measurements do the job.
It has 6 faces, in 3 equal pairs.

blocks.content: Know the properties, and shape problems become simple counting. Let's practise!
